claim: The TREM2 crystal structure was determined at 3.1 Å resolution.
source: We determined the crystal structure of the TREM2 ectodomain at 3.1 Å resolution
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of the crystal structure in the abstract and results sections, with supporting crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: Nasu-Hakola disease mutations in TREM2 are buried within the protein structure.
source: The side chains of mutations causing NHD (Y38, T66 and V126) are all buried within the core of the Ig fold
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis showing low solvent accessibility values in Figure 1c.

claim: Alzheimer's disease risk variants in TREM2 are found on the protein surface.
source: the side chains of verified AD risk variants (R47H and R62H) and possible AD risk variants (N68K, D87N and T96K) all lie on the protein surface
evidence: This is directly stated in the results section and supported by structural analysis showing high solvent accessibility values in Figure 1c.

claim: The TREM2 R47H variant is associated with Alzheimer's disease risk similar to that of APOE4.
source: In particular, the TREM2 R47H variant is associated with a risk that is similar to that associated with APOE4, previously the only well-established risk factor for late-onset AD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior genetic studies mentioned in the introduction.

claim: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on dendritic cells, resident macrophages, osteoclasts, microglia, infiltrating macrophages, inflammatory macrophages, and CSF monocytes.
source: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on dendritic cells (DCs), resident macrophages such as osteoclasts and microglia, infiltrating (Jay et al., 2015) and inflammatory (Wu et al., 2015) macrophages, and CSF monocytes (Colonna and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to prior literature.

claim: TREM2 is a type one receptor protein consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, a short stalk, a transmembrane domain that associates with DAP12, and a cytoplasmic tail.
source: It is a type one receptor protein consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, a short stalk, a transmembrane domain that associates with the adaptor protein DAP12 for signaling, and a cytoplasmic tail (Figure 1a) (Colonna, 2003).
evidence: This structural description is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1a and supported by citation.

claim: The TREM2 ectodomain contains two disulfide bonds: one canonical Ig disulfide between C36 and C110, and an additional linkage between C51 and C60.
source: The TREM2 ectodomain is a V-type Ig domain containing two disulfide bonds, the canonical Ig disulfide between residues C36 and C110 (βB–βF) and an additional linkage between C51 and C60 (βC-βC') (Figure 1b).
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the crystal structure and described in the results section.

claim: A single N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) glycan is visible at residue N79 in the TREM2 crystal structure.
source: A single N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) glycan that remains after Endo Hf treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a) is clearly visible in the electron density at residue N79 (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron density maps shown in the figures.

claim: The TREM2 asymmetric unit contains two monomers in a parallel arrangement.
source: The asymmetric unit (ASU) contains two monomers of hTREM2 in a parallel arrangement, but the limited buried surface area (~400 Å2) and chemical nature of the interface suggest that this dimer would not exist in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure and analyzed for biological relevance.

claim: The two TREM2 monomers in the asymmetric unit are structurally similar with a Cα RMSD of 0.65 Å.
source: Furthermore, these two monomers are quite similar (Cα RMSD of 0.65 Å, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is a quantitative structural comparison directly calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: Y38 is adjacent to C36 which forms an intramolecular disulfide with C110, so the Y38C mutation likely disrupts correct disulfide formation.
source: Y38 is adjacent to C36, which forms an intramolecular disulfide with C110, so the Y38C mutation most likely disrupts correct disulfide formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of the Y38 position relative to the disulfide bond.

claim: T66 is tightly packed inside the core of the protein with the side chain hydroxyl engaging the backbone amide of K48.
source: T66 immediately follows the C' β-sheet and is tightly packed inside the core of the protein, with the side chain hydroxyl engaging the backbone amide of K48 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The T66M mutation would sterically disrupt packing and probably destabilize the protein.
source: The T66M mutation would sterically disrupt this packing and probably destabilize the protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of the T66 position and the expected effect of the methionine substitution.

claim: V126 is entirely buried and contributes to a hydrophobic core with residues F24, D104, A105, and Y108.
source: V126 is located on β-sheet G; it is entirely buried and contributes to a hydrophobic core of the buried residues F24, D104, A105, and Y108.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The V126G mutation would disrupt hydrophobic core packing and probably destabilize this core.
source: Removal of the side chain by the V126G mutation would disrupt this packing and probably destabilize this hydrophobic core (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis of the V126 position and the expected effect of the glycine substitution.

claim: Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family.
source: In addition, sequence analysis reveals that Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family, implying that they are probably required to preserve the common fold within this family of receptors (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: T66 is less conserved in the TREM family but highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
source: The T66 residue is less conserved in the TREM family, but is highly conserved in TREM2 proteins across species.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis across TREM family members and TREM2 orthologs.

claim: R47 is at the end of the loop preceding β-sheet C and is well-ordered in the structure with the side chain lying parallel along the surface.
source: R47, the residue with the strongest link to AD as the R47H variant, is at the end of the loop preceding β-sheet C. It is well-ordered in the structure with the side chain lying parallel along the surface of the protein, and the side-chain amines engage the carbonyl oxygen of T66 (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: N68 is surface exposed and its side chain makes no obvious polar contacts within the molecule.
source: N68 is also surface exposed and its side chain makes no obvious polar contacts within the molecule.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: D87 is at the end of β-strand D with its side chain extending from the protein surface, and the side-chain carboxyl engages the backbone amide of G90.
source: D87 is at the end of β-strand D; its side chain extends from the protein surface and the side-chain carboxyl engages the backbone amide of G90. This interaction probably stabilizes the βD-E loop.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure with inference about functional significance.

claim: T96 is on the end of β-strand E and its side chain points away from the surface and engages the side chain of Q33.
source: T96 is on the end of β-strand E and its side chain points away from the surface and engages the side chain of Q33 (Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: WT hTREM2 ectodomain consistently eluted as a monomer in size exclusion chromatography.
source: WT hTREM2 ectodomain consistently eluted as a monomer (Figure 2a and b), in accordance with our crystallographic analysis.
evidence: This is directly observed in the size exclusion chromatography experiments shown in Figure 2a.

claim: All TREM2 AD risk variant ectodomains (R47H, R62H, N68K, D87N, T96K) elute at the same volume as WT TREM2.
source: The verified (R47H and R62H) and possible (N68K, D87N and T96K) AD-risk variants all elute at the same volume as WT TREM2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g–l), suggesting that these mutations do not drastically alter the folding or oligomerization of TREM2 in solution.
evidence: This is directly observed in the size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: All TREM2 AD risk variant ectodomains migrated as monomers in the absence of reducing agent.
source: Furthermore, all of the TREM2 AD risk variant ectodomains migrated as monomers in the absence of reducing agent (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2b.

claim: TREM2 NHD mutants (Y38C, T66M, V126G) elute much earlier than WT in size exclusion chromatography, consistent with aggregation and misfolding.
source: By contrast, although the buried NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G were secreted, they elute much earlier, consistent with aggregation and misfolding of these proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1m–o).
evidence: This is directly observed in the size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: TREM2 NHD mutants were largely produced as covalent dimers or trimers under non-reducing conditions, indicating misfolding promoted aberrant intermolecular disulfide bonds.
source: Consistent with this observation, SDS-PAGE analysis of TREM2 NHD mutants in the absence of reducing agent showed that these ectodomains were largely produced as covalent dimers or trimers, indicating that misfolding of these mutants promoted the formation of aberrant intermolecular disulfide bonds (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Anti-TREM2 staining was decreased for the NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G.
source: However, as predicted by our structural analysis, anti-TREM2 staining was decreased for the NHD mutants Y38C, T66M, and V126G, but not for the AD risk variants R47H, R62H, N68K, D87N, and T96K (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Anti-FLAG antibody showed surface expression for all TREM2 mutants.
source: By contrast, the anti-FLAG antibody showed surface expression for all TREM2 mutants (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The NHD mutant Y38C displayed diffuse intracellular accumulation in permeabilized cells, in comparison to WT and R47H which displayed a distinct punctate staining pattern.
source: We found that the surface expression pattern in non-permeabilized cells was similar for all cell types, whereas in permeabilized cells, the NHD mutant Y38C displayed diffuse intracellular accumulation, in comparison to WT and R47H which displayed a distinct punctate staining pattern (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is directly observed in the confocal microscopy experiments shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates were found when expressing full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells.
source: Consistent with these observations, we found significant amounts of SDS-resistant aggregates by anti-FLAG immunoblotting when expressing the full-length TREM2 NHD mutants in 293T cells (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is directly observed in the immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Both Y38C and R47H TREM2 variants have some signaling potential but neither sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2.
source: Consistent with our observation of FLAG-TREM2 on the cell surface for all the variant proteins, we found that while both the Y38C and R47H variants have some signaling potential, as assessed by phosphorylated-ERK blotting in RAW264.7 and Cos-7 cells, neither of these variants sustains signaling as efficiently as WT TREM2 (Figure 2i,j).
evidence: This is directly observed in the phospho-ERK immunoblot experiments shown in Figure 2i and 2j.

claim: R47H showed a subtle but statistically significant difference in the 214 nm/233 nm CD ratio compared to WT.
source: We found that R62H and T96K displayed CD spectra similar to WT proteins while, surprisingly, R47H showed a subtle, yet statistically significant difference in the 214 nm/233 nm ratio (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the CD spectroscopy experiments shown in Figure 3a and 3b.

claim: The R47H mutation in TREM2 induces a small but measurable conformational change.
source: Thus the R47H mutation in TREM2 seems to induce a small, but measurable, conformational change, whereas the R62H and T96K mutations do not induce any structural changes detectable by CD.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD spectroscopy data showing differences in the 214/233 nm ratio.

claim: Each TREM2 surface variant produced slightly lower denaturation temperatures by DSF, with T96K having the lowest.
source: Each surface variant produced slightly lower denaturation temperatures, with R47H and R62H marginally reduced when compared to WT proteins and T96K having the lowest denaturation temperatures (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the DSF experiments shown in Figure 3c.

claim: WT TREM2 and all TREM2 variants tested showed reversible thermal denaturation by CD.
source: WT TREM2 and all the TREM2 variants tested showed reversible thermal denaturation as they reacquired their native spectra rapidly after cooling from 90°C to 20°C, but their ability to refold was ablated in the presence of DTT (not shown).
evidence: This is directly observed in the thermal denaturation CD experiments.

claim: Thermal denaturation by CD did not show a difference between WT, R47H, and R62H proteins, but T96K had a pronounced shift towards lower denaturation temperature.
source: In contrast to DSF measurements, thermal denaturation by CD did not show a difference between WT, R47H, and R62H proteins; however, the T96K variant has a pronounced shift towards lower denaturation temperature (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is directly observed in the thermal denaturation CD experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: R47H and R62H proteins melt at slightly lower GuHCl concentrations than WT protein, while T96K unfolds at lower GuHCl concentrations than R47H and R62H.
source: The R47H and R62H proteins melt at slightly lower GuHCl concentrations than the WT protein, while the T96K variant unfolds at lower GuHCl concentrations than R47H and R62H, consistent with the thermal melt experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the chemical denaturation experiments.

claim: No differences in phospholipid discrimination or direct lipid binding were observed between WT and AD variant TREM2 ectodomains.
source: However, we did not observe differences in phospholipid discrimination or in direct lipid binding between WT and AD variant TREM2 ectodomains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the phospholipid binding assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both human and mouse TREM2/SA-PE tetramers were able to bind Neuro2A (N2A) and THP-1 cells.
source: In initial experiments, we found that both human and mouse TREM2/SA-PE tetramers were able to bind Neuro2A (N2A) and THP-1 cells (Figure 4b–d,f,g and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in the figures.

claim: Overnight treatment with PMA/ionomycin dramatically decreased binding of TREM2/SA-PE tetramers to THP-1 cells.
source: To validate the specificity of our reagent, we cultured THP-1 cells with various immune stimuli and found that overnight treatment with PMA/ionomycin dramatically decreased binding of TREM2/SA-PE tetramers to THP-1 cells (Figure 4b and c), while the myeloid cell marker CD45 remained unchanged (not shown).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 4b and 4c.

claim: TREM2 binding is sensitive to proteinase treatment of cells.
source: We next sought to interrogate the endogenous target recognized by TREM2 on the cell surface, and found that TREM2 binding is sensitive to proteinase treatment of cells prior to incubation with our staining reagent (Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Treatment with proteinase K abolished TREM2 binding while chymotrypsin and elastase had an intermediate effect.
source: Treatment with proteinase K abolished binding while the more specific proteases chymotrypsin and elastase had an intermediate effect.
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments.

claim: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-AAD staining.
source: Proteinase K treatment did not affect cell viability, which was >99% by 7-aminoactinomycin D (7-AAD) staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the viability assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2f.

claim: TREM2-L contains a protein component.
source: This demonstrates that TREM2-L contains a protein component.
evidence: This is inferred from the protease sensitivity experiments showing that protease treatment reduces TREM2 binding.

claim: GAG-dependent cell binding of the TREM2 tetramer was observed in CHO-K1 cells but not in GAG-deficient CHO-745 cells.
source: We tested binding to wild-type CHO-K1 cells, which express heparan and chondroitin sulfates, and to CHO-745 cells, which are deficient in GAG maturation and surface expression (Esko et al., 1985). In this experiment, GAG-dependent cell binding of the TREM2 tetramer was observed (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Treatment with heparinases had a pronounced effect on TREM2 cell surface binding while chondroitinase only slightly diminished binding in CHO, THP-1, and N2A cells.
source: In CHO (Figure 4e), THP-1 (Figure 4f) and N2A (Figure 4g) cells, treatment with heparinases had a pronounced effect on cell surface binding while chondroitinase only slightly diminished binding, together implicating GAGs, specifically heparin sulfate, as a major component of the cell surface TREM2-L.
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figures 4e, 4f, and 4g.

claim: The AD-linked variant R47H displayed markedly diminished binding to N2A and THP-1 cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the AD-linked variant R47H displayed markedly diminished binding to N2A and THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell binding experiments using multiple formats.

claim: The T96K variant significantly increased binding to N2A and THP-1 cells.
source: In stark contrast, the potentially AD-protective T96K variant significantly increased binding.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell binding experiments using multiple formats.

claim: The R62H variant reduced binding as measured in the anti-6H format, but the reduction was less dramatic when measured by competition or tetramer staining.
source: The R62H variant reduced binding as measured in the anti-6H format, but the reduction in binding was less dramatic when measured by competition or tetramer staining, suggesting an intermediate decrease in affinity.
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing results across different binding assay formats.

claim: TREM2 has a large basic surface that is not present on other TREM family receptors.
source: Upon mapping the electrostatic surface of hTREM2, we noticed a large basic surface that was not present on the surface of other TREM family receptors for which coordinates are available (mTREM1, PDB 1 U9K, [Kelker et al., 2004a]; hTREM1, PDB 1SMO, [Kelker et al., 2004b]; and TLT-1, PDB 2FRG [Gattis et al., 2006]) (Figure 5a,b and d–f).
evidence: This is observed through electrostatic surface analysis and comparison with other TREM family structures.

claim: The residues constituting the basic patch on TREM2 are highly conserved within TREM2 but not within the rest of the TREM family.
source: Furthermore, sequence analysis shows that the residues constituting this basic patch are highly conserved within TREM2, but not within the rest of the TREM family, suggesting that this interface has evolved specifically toward a role in TREM2 function (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: TREM2 ectodomain tetramers bound to N2A cells, while tetramers of TREML2 and TREML4 ectodomains did not.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, TREM2 ectodomain tetramers bound to N2A cells, while tetramers of ectodomains from TREM-like 2 (TREML2) and TREM-like 4 (TREML4) did not (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 4i.

claim: The T96K mutation is located adjacent to the basic patch and would extend it, providing a structural explanation for the gain of function observed with this variant.
source: Additionally, the T96K mutation is located adjacent to this basic patch and would therefore extend it, providing a structural explanation for the gain of function observed with this variant (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the T96 position relative to the basic patch and the observed gain of binding function.

claim: Both R76D and R77D mutations decreased binding to TREM2-L on THP-1 cells in a manner similar to the validated AD risk variants.
source: We found that both a R76D and a R77D mutation decreased binding to TREM2-L on THP-1 cells in a manner similar to the validated AD risk variants (R47H and R62H) (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is directly observed in the flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 5g.

claim: NHD-linked mutant residues are buried and impact protein folding and stability.
source: Our studies indicate, as presaged by our crystal structure, that NHD-linked mutant residues are buried and impact protein folding and stability
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis, SEC, SDS-PAGE, and surface expression data.

claim: AD-linked variant residues are on the protein surface and do not diminish the stability or surface expression of the molecule but instead impact ligand engagement.
source: while AD-linked variant residues are on the protein surface and do not diminish the stability or surface expression of the molecule but instead impact ligand engagement (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis, stability measurements, surface expression data, and ligand binding assays.

claim: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia.
source: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia, and the absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, which was correlated with increased accumulation of Aβ plaques (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior studies in AD mouse models.

claim: The absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, which was correlated with increased accumulation of Aβ plaques.
source: TREM2-deficient AD mice display fewer activated microglia, and the absence of TREM2 prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, which was correlated with increased accumulation of Aβ plaques (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior studies in AD mouse models.

claim: Microglia in TREM2-deficient AD mice displayed less activation and did not engulf Aβ plaques.
source: Microglia in TREM2-deficient AD mice displayed less activation and did not engulf Aβ plaques.
evidence: This is cited from prior studies in AD mouse models.

claim: The absence of TREM2 impacts the density of Aβ plaques and promotes diffuse Aβ structures, which are more neurotoxic.
source: This impacts the density of Aβ plaques and promotes diffuse Aβ structures, which in turn are more neurotoxic, and contributes to the accumulation of classic AD pathology (Wang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior studies in AD mouse models.

claim: TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic (PA, PG, PI, PS) over more neutral (PC, PE) lipids.
source: In contrast to highly selective phospholipid binding by other Ig domains (Kobayashi et al., 2007; Miyanishi et al., 2007; Santiago et al., 2007; Simhadri et al., 2012), purified TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic (PA, PG, PI, PS) over more neutral (PC, PE) lipids (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a,b and c).
evidence: This is directly observed in the phospholipid binding ELISA and liposome sedimentation assays.

claim: TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike TIM and CD300 proteins.
source: Moreover, while TREM2 does share a conserved aspartic acid residue from this motif, which chelates a required Ca2+ ion for the TIM and CD300a proteins, TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike TIM and CD300 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e and f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the lipid binding experiments with divalent metal ions and EDTA.

claim: There is a long and narrow hydrophobic patch on the end of TREM2 most distal from the plasma membrane that is the most likely lipid-binding surface.
source: By contrast, it should be noted that there is a long and narrow hydrophobic patch on the end of TREM2 most distal from the plasma membrane (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) that is the most likely lipid-binding surface.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the hydrophobic surface properties of TREM2.

claim: The hydrophobic patch on TREM2 is adjacent to the basic patch, which could mediate interaction with anionic phospholipid head groups.
source: Interestingly this patch is adjacent to the basic patch, which could mediate interaction with anionic phospholipid head groups (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing the spatial relationship between the hydrophobic and basic patches.

claim: TREM2 interaction with GAGs in cis is likely required to orient or cluster TREM2 to mediate signaling upon stimulation by phospholipids.
source: As the R47H risk variant is able to bind phospholipids directly, but does not signal in cellular assays of TREM2 signaling triggered by plated phospholipids (Wang et al., 2015), we suggest that TREM2 interaction with GAGs in cis is likely required to orient or cluster TREM2 to mediate signaling upon stimulation by phospholipids.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R47H binds phospholipids but doesn't signal, combined with the finding that R47H has reduced GAG binding.

claim: Phospholipids may function to orient TREM2 on the cell surface for proper presentation to GAGs and/or additional protein surface receptors.
source: Alternatively, phospholipids may function to orient TREM2 on the cell surface for proper presentation to GAGs and/or additional as of yet undefined protein surface receptors.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential role of phospholipids in TREM2 function.

claim: The TREM2 R47H mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau levels.
source: This mutation correlates with increased cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau levels, a well-established risk factor for AD (Cruchaga et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from prior clinical studies.

claim: The TREM2 R47H mutation has been identified in patients with frontal temporal dementia (FTD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: and subsequent studies have identified this mutation in patients who have frontal temporal dementia (FTD), Parkinson's disease (PD) (Rayaprolu et al., 2013), and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Cady et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior clinical studies.

claim: Microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are the most significantly dysregulated in late-onset AD.
source: A recent study of more than 1,600 late-onset AD (LOAD) and cognitively normal brains revealed that microglia-specific networks, including those containing TREM2, are those most significantly dysregulated in LOAD (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from a prior large-scale brain study.

claim: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines from bone-marrow-derived macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: TREM2 has historically been shown to play an anti-inflammatory role in vitro by antagonizing the production of inflammatory cytokines from bone-marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and dendritic cells (BMDDCs) in response to FcR (Hamerman et al., 2006) and Tlr signaling (Turnbull et al., 2006; Ito and Hamerman, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from prior in vitro studies.

claim: TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Likewise, TREM2 participates in phagocytosis of apoptotic cells in cultured microglia and reduces the production of inflammatory cytokines (Takahashi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from prior in vitro studies.

claim: TREM2-expressing macrophages can promote inflammatory disease in the brain and lung.
source: However, TREM2-expressing macrophages can also promote inflammatory disease in the brain (Jay et al., 2015) and lung (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior in vivo studies.

claim: Homozygous mutations in TREM2 including early-stop codons, splice site mutations, and specific coding mutations cause Nasu-Hakola disease or frontotemporal dementia.
source: Homozygous mutations including early-stop codons (Paloneva et al., 2003; Soragna et al., 2003), splice site mutations (Numasawa et al., 2011; Chouery et al., 2008), the coding stalk mutations D134G and K186N (Paloneva et al., 2002), and the coding ectodomain mutations Y38C, T66M, and V126G (Guerreiro et al., 2013a, 2013c; Le Ber et al., 2014) cause either NHD, characterized by early-onset dementia, demyelination, and bone cyst lipoma (Paloneva et al., 2002; Colonna, 2003), or a frontotemporal dementia variant with severe loss of brain matter but lacking the bone manifestations.
evidence: This is cited from prior genetic and clinical studies.

claim: TREM2 mutations associated with AD contribute to disease risk as heterozygous variants.
source: By contrast, TREM2 mutations associated with AD contribute to disease risk as heterozygous variants.
evidence: This is based on genetic studies showing heterozygous inheritance patterns for AD risk variants.

claim: R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies.
source: In addition to R47H, the coding mutation R62H is associated with increased risk of AD in independent studies (Jin et al., 2014; Ridge et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior genetic association studies.

claim: N68K and D87N have been identified in AD patients, but their risk remains uncertain due to rarity.
source: N68K and D87N have also been identified in AD patients, but because these mutations are very rare, their risk remains uncertain (Guerreiro et al., 2013b; Jonsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from prior genetic studies with acknowledgment of statistical limitations.

claim: The T96K mutation has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is too rare to allow verification.
source: In addition, the mutation T96K has been linked to a decreased risk of AD, but this mutation is also too rare to allow verification of this observation (Jin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from prior genetic studies with acknowledgment of statistical limitations.

claim: The TREM2 ectodomain contains nine β-strands characteristic of V-type Ig domains.
source: The nine β-strands characteristic of proteins within this Ig domain class are present, and two short α-helix passages are observed spanning β-sheets B–C and E–F.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Two short α-helix passages are observed in TREM2 spanning β-sheets B–C and E–F.
source: The nine β-strands characteristic of proteins within this Ig domain class are present, and two short α-helix passages are observed spanning β-sheets B–C and E–F.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The TREM2 structure is complete with only one N-terminal residue and four C-terminal residues not visible in the electron density.
source: The structure is complete with only one N-terminal residue and four C-terminal residues not visible in the electron density (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the completeness of the structural model based on electron density.

claim: Ramachandran statistics for the TREM2 structure are 97.7% favored, 0% outliers, 2.3% allowed.
source: Ramachandran statistics are 97.7% favored, 0% outliers, 2.3% allowed.
evidence: This is a quality metric calculated from the refined crystal structure.

claim: The Molprobity score for the TREM2 structure was 1.66 (100th percentile) and clashscore was 9.62 (96th percentile).
source: Molprobity score was 1.66 (100th percentile) and clashscore was 9.62 (96th percentile) for the final model.
evidence: This is a quality metric calculated from the refined crystal structure.

claim: Whole-cell expression levels of the TREM2 NHD mutants were slightly higher than those of WT or AD risk variant TREM2.
source: Whole-cell expression levels of the TREM2 NHD mutants were slightly higher than those of WT or AD risk variant TREM2 (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is directly observed in the western blot analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: There have been reports of rare AD cases containing heterozygous NHD variants, including Q33X, Y38C, and T66M.
source: Consistent with this, there have been reports of rare AD cases containing heterozygous NHD variants, including Q33X, Y38C, and T66M (Guerreiro et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is cited from prior clinical case reports.

claim: Soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages.
source: We have recently shown that the soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by the authors.

claim: The absence of TREM2 in an AD mouse model prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, we have observed that the absence of TREM2 in an AD mouse model prevents microglia proliferation and promotes microglia apoptosis, suggesting that soluble TREM2 could play a similar role in the CNS (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by the authors in AD mouse models.

claim: Soluble TREM2 can be detected in the CNS.
source: Accordingly, soluble TREM2 can be detected in the CNS, and we have shown that some AD risk variants, but not the NHD mutant proteins are readily detected in the CSF of patients (Piccio et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by the authors measuring soluble TREM2 in patient CSF.

claim: Some AD risk variants, but not NHD mutant proteins, are readily detected in the CSF of patients.

claim: TREM2 was reported to bind lipid-loaded ApoE and this interaction facilitates uptake of Aβ loaded into lipoparticles by microglia.
source: On that note, while this manuscript was in preparation, it was reported that TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE and that this interaction facilitates uptake of Aβ loaded into lipoparticles by microglia (Yeh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a concurrent study published while this manuscript was in preparation.

claim: TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE according to a recent report.
source: This report also suggests that TREM2 AD risk variants decrease binding to ApoE, but binding affinities were not quantitated.
evidence: This is cited from a concurrent study, with a note about limitations of the data.

claim: The basic patch on TREM2 contains most of the AD-linked surface mutations including R47H and R62H.
source: This cluster of residues contains most of the AD-linked surface mutations (including R47H and R62H).
evidence: This is observed through structural mapping of disease mutations onto the basic patch surface.
